recall_prompt: Say how you would count the diagonals of a twelve-sided polygon — where the formula comes from, and the number.
insider_note: ¹²C₂ counts every join of two vertices, sides included, so the sides must be subtracted: 66 − 12 = 54. The subtraction line is the first mark — the formula n(n − 3)/2 is that subtraction already done.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Diagonals = all joins minus the sides
steps.margin_note: First mark. Any 2 of the n vertices give a line, ⁿC₂; n of those lines are sides. Diagonals = ⁿC₂ − n = n(n − 3)/2.
steps.memory_tip: ⁿC₂ counts every join of two vertices, and n of those are sides. Diagonals = ⁿC₂ − n = n(n − 3)/2.
lines: A polygon with n sides has n vertices.
Joining any 2 vertices gives a line:
Of these, n lines are the sides themselves,

recall.must_convey: That the diagonals are the joins of two vertices, n C 2, minus the n sides, which simplifies to n times n minus 3 over 2.
accept: n C two joins minus the n sides gives n into n minus three by two
diagonals equal n C two minus n
the formula is n times n minus three over two
n C two minus n, adi n into n minus three by two
every pair of vertices is a line, take away the sides

steps.why: The formula is not a separate fact: ⁿC₂ counts every segment joining two vertices, and the only such segments that are not diagonals are the n sides. Knowing that derivation is what lets a student reconstruct n(n − 3)/2 in the exam.
common_mistakes: Using ⁿC₂ alone and forgetting to subtract the sides.
Writing n(n − 1)/2 (which is ⁿC₂) instead of n(n − 3)/2.

steps.label: Evaluate for n = 12

accept: twelve into nine by two is fifty four
twelve times nine is one hundred eight, half is fifty four
twelve into nine by two fifty four
the answer is fifty four diagonals

steps.why: Check with the alternative form: ¹²C₂ − 12 = 66 − 12 = 54, the same number.
